question: A 27-year-old woman goes to the genetic counseling clinic after having a child with Down syndrome. In the child, a trisomy 21 with translocation 21/21 inherited from the mother is identified. What would be the risk of recurrence of Down syndrome in the future children of this woman?

options.opa: The risk of recurrence will be 10-15%, as in the rest of translocations.
options.opb: 100% of viable fetuses will be born with Down syndrome.
options.opc: The risk of recurrence will be very low (12%).
options.opd: The risk of recurrence will be 50%.

enhanced_information: The mother has a child with Down syndrome due to a trisomy 21 with a translocation 21/21, which indicates a genetic predisposition to Down syndrome. In cases of Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21, the recurrence risk for future pregnancies can be significantly higher than the general population risk. Specifically, for a maternal translocation 21/21, the risk of recurrence is approximately 100% for viable pregnancies, as any viable fetus will inherit the translocated chromosome leading to Down syndrome. Therefore, the correct interpretation of the risk of recurrence for this woman is that 100% of viable fetuses will be born with Down syndrome.
analysis: In cases of Down syndrome caused by a Robertsonian translocation, the risk of recurrence depends on whether the translocation is balanced or unbalanced. In this scenario, the mother has a translocation 21/21, which is an unbalanced translocation. This means that any viable offspring will inherit the extra chromosome 21, leading to a 100% risk of Down syndrome in future pregnancies. Therefore, the most accurate option is that 100% of viable fetuses will be born with Down syndrome.
